newsitem.title: TAIWAN: EU anti-dumping duty cheers Taiwan chipmakers.
newsitem.headline: EU anti-dumping duty cheers Taiwan chipmakers.

text.p: Taiwan officials and chipmakers on Tuesday welcomed a European Commission decision to impose anti-dumping duties on Japanese and Korean microchip exports, saying it would benefit local high-tech firms.
"The decision should be a plus for the development of our chip industry because we are not included," a spokesman of the cabinet's Board of Foreign Trade told Reuters by telephone.
The EU said on Monday that it was reintroducing minimum prices -- in effect setting anti-dumping duties -- on DRAM chips from Japan and South Korea, Taiwan's main competitors.
The Taiwan spokesman said the decision should help boost orders for rival chipmakers in Taiwan.
TI-Acer Inc, Nan Ya Technology and other major Taiwan chipmakers also welcomed the EU move.
"It's more bullish than bearish to us because it will help boost our competitiveness," said TI-Acer spokeswoman Ruth Pao.
"The measures should be able to boost local DRAM prices, which have remained painfully low for some time and only recently began a gradual rebound.
Taiwan analysts said the EU had no choice but to impose the anti-dumping tax because of the stiff competition from Japan and South Korea.
But they also warned of harmful effects of such a tax, calling it a protectionist practice that in the long run would also hurt Taiwan.
The measure takes effect on April 1 and duties will be introduced gradually to avoid harming the EU chip market, where DRAM prices have been low.
EU officials declined to say how much duty the organisation wanted from the measures, which will target 12 Japanese and three Korean companies.
The EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Japanese exports in January 1990 and on Korean exports later. The measures were suspended 21 months ago.
The EU market for DRAM chips was worth five billion European currency units (US$5.7 billion) in 1995.
